emergency.ateCaffeine.science.content: La cafeína (1,3,7-trimetilxantina) es un antagonista del receptor de adenosina e inhibidor de la fosfodiesterasa. En los perros, provoca la estimulación del sistema nervioso central, la contracción del músculo cardíaco y la relajación del músculo liso. Los perros metabolizan la cafeína mucho más lentamente que los humanos: la vida media en los perros es de 4,5 horas frente a 3 horas en los humanos. Esto prolonga los efectos tóxicos. En dosis altas, la cafeína causa una liberación excesiva de catecolaminas que conduce a taquicardia, fibrilación y potencialmente la muerte (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateChocolate.science.content: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, both methylxanthines that dogs metabolize much more slowly than humans. While humans eliminate theobromine in 2-3 hours, dogs take 17.5 hours or more. This allows toxic levels to build up in their system. Theobromine affects the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, and smooth muscles. At high doses, it causes seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions contain thiosulfate compounds (n-propyl disulfide) that dogs cannot metabolize. These compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, forming Heinz bodies — damaged hemoglobin that precipitates inside the cell. The spleen then destroys these damaged cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This process takes 1-3 days, which is why symptoms are delayed (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateSock.science.content: Fabric foreign bodies are particularly dangerous because they can become lodged at the pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) or in the small intestine. Once stuck, they cause a complete blockage — nothing can pass, and the intestinal wall may become necrotic (die) from pressure. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, and death without surgical intervention. Puppies and small dogs are at highest risk due to their narrower intestinal diameter (AVMA, 2023).

emergency.ateAntifreeze.science.content: Ethylene glycol itself is not toxic — it is the metabolites produced by the liver that cause damage. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, then oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that destroy kidney tissue. This process causes metabolic acidosis and acute kidney failure within 12-36 hours. The antidote works by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.question: Are avocados toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.answer: Avocado contains persin, a fungicidal toxin that is mildly toxic to dogs. The flesh causes mild GI upset in most dogs, but the pit (seed) poses a far greater danger as it can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The skin and leaves also contain higher persin concentrations than the flesh.

emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate an avocado pit?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.answer: If your dog swallowed an avocado pit, contact your vet immediately. The pit is large enough to cause intestinal blockage, especially in small and medium dogs. Do NOT induce vomiting — the pit can lodge in the esophagus on the way back up. Your vet will X-ray to locate the pit and determine if surgical removal is needed.

emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.question: How much avocado is dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.answer: The flesh has low toxicity — most dogs experience only mild vomiting or diarrhea from eating avocado flesh. However, the pit is a choking hazard and obstruction risk regardless of amount. The leaves and skin contain higher persin levels and should be avoided. Pancreatitis risk increases with large amounts due to high fat content.

emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.question: Can dogs eat guacamole?
emergency.ateAvocado.faqs.answer: No, guacamole is especially dangerous for dogs because it typically contains onion, garlic, lime juice, and salt — all of which are toxic to dogs. Onion and garlic cause hemolytic anemia, salt can cause ion poisoning, and lime peel contains essential oils. Call your vet immediately if your dog ate guacamole.

emergency.ateAvocado.vetDecision.urgent: Pit swallowed in a small dog (< 15 lbs)
Large amount of flesh eaten (pancreatitis risk)
Persistent vomiting or diarrhea beyond 12 hours
emergency.ateAvocado.vetDecision.monitor: Small amount of flesh eaten with no symptoms
Mild single episode of vomiting or diarrhea

emergency.ateCaffeine.riskAssessment.row.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW for small dogs
📞 Call vet or poison control immediately

emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.title: Step 1: Act Fast — Caffeine Absorbs Quickly
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.content: Remove any remaining caffeine source. Caffeine is absorbed within 30-60 minutes — time is critical for decontamination.

emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control or Vet Immediately
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Have the product label ready to report caffeine content in mg.

emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptoms Present
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.content: ⚠️ If your dog shows trembling, hyperactivity, or seizures, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 30 minutes of ingestion.

emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.title: Step 4: Monitor Heart and Breathing
emergency.ateCaffeine.steps.content: Watch for rapid breathing, restlessness, and elevated heart rate. Caffeine causes cardiac arrhythmias — if your dog collapses or has difficulty breathing, go to emergency vet NOW.

emergency.ateCaffeine.timeline.description: Early signs: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate
Severe signs: tremors, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, collapse
Resolution with treatment: hospitalization typically required 24-48 hours; good prognosis with early care

emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.question: How much caffeine is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.answer: Mild symptoms appear at 20mg/kg of body weight. Severe toxicity occurs at 60mg/kg. The lethal dose (LD50) is approximately 140mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals roughly 2,800mg of caffeine — about 28 cups of coffee. However, even small amounts (1-2 caffeine pills of 200mg each) can cause serious symptoms in small dogs.

emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of caffeine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 1-2 hours and include: restlessness, hyperactivity, vomiting, elevated heart rate, tremors, seizures, and collapse. Caffeine is absorbed rapidly and affects the central nervous system and cardiovascular system. Severe cases cause cardiac arrhythmias that can be fatal.

emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate caffeine?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, caffeine is rapidly absorbed and can cause seizures — never induce vomiting if your dog shows any neurological symptoms. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for guidance.

emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.question: What is the treatment for caffeine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateCaffeine.faqs.answer: Treatment includes: induced vomiting (if early), activated charcoal to reduce absorption, IV fluids for elimination, anti-arrhythmic medications for heart issues, anti-seizure medications, and temperature regulation. Hospitalization is typically required for 24-48 hours. Prognosis is good with early treatment.

emergency.ateCaffeine.vetDecision.emerge: Inability to stand with elevated heart rate

emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.title: Step 1: Remove All Alcohol Immediately
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.content: Take away any remaining beverages, food containing alcohol, or raw bread dough. Clean up any spills — dogs may lick floors.

emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.title: Step 2: Assess Your Dog's Neurological State
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.content: Check: Can your dog walk normally? Are they alert or depressed? Vomiting? If your dog cannot stand or is unconscious — go to emergency vet NOW.

emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.title: Step 3: Call Poison Control
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Calculate approximate alcohol consumed in grams: volume (mL) × alcohol% × 0.789 = grams of ethanol.

emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.title: Step 4: Keep Your Dog Safe
emergency.ateAlcohol.steps.content: Prevent falls due to ataxia. Keep your dog warm — alcohol causes vasodilation and hypothermia. Do NOT leave them unattended. Monitor breathing and consciousness every 15 minutes.

emergency.ateAlcohol.timeline.description: Early signs: disorientation, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting, depression
Severe signs: slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia (especially small dogs/puppies)
Resolution with supportive care: IV fluids, glucose, blood pH monitoring; unmonitored cases risk coma or death

emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.question: Is alcohol toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.answer: Yes, alcohol (ethanol) is highly toxic to dogs. The lethal dose is 5.5 mL/kg of pure ethanol. Dogs are much more sensitive than humans because they lack efficient alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes. Even small amounts cause ataxia, depression, and metabolic acidosis. Beer, wine, liquor, and raw bread dough all pose serious risks.

emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of alcohol poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: disorientation, loss of coordination (ataxia), vomiting, depression, slowed breathing, metabolic acidosis, and in severe cases, coma and death. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is a dangerous complication, especially in small dogs and puppies.

emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.question: Can beer kill a dog?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.answer: Yes, beer can kill a dog. A single 12oz beer (5% alcohol = 17g ethanol) can cause severe intoxication in a small dog (under 10kg). Dogs metabolize alcohol much slower than humans, so effects accumulate. Carbonation also speeds absorption. Never intentionally give alcohol to dogs.

emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.question: What should I do if my dog accidentally drank alcohol?
emergency.ateAlcohol.faqs.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog shows neurological symptoms (depression, ataxia). Remove any remaining alcohol. Keep your dog warm and safe from falls. Your vet may need to administer IV fluids, glucose, and monitor blood pH.

emergency.ateAlcohol.vetDecision.emergen: Unconsciousness or inability to be roused
Severe ataxia with inability to stand
emergency.ateAlcohol.vetDecision.urgent: Known ingestion of raw bread dough
emergency.ateAlcohol.vetDecision.monitor: Alert and walking normally after 1 hour

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.riskAssessmen.action: 📞 Call vet or poison control immediately
👀 Monitor for symptoms, call vet if concerned

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.title: Step 1: Don't Panic, But Act Quickly
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.content: Remove any remaining macadamia nuts from your dog's reach. Stay calm — your dog will pick up on your stress.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.title: Step 2: Do NOT Induce Vomiting (Unless Instructed)
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.content: ⚠️ Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia. Only induce vomiting if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian or poison control.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.title: Step 3: Gather Critical Information
items: Estimate the amount consumed (count wrappers, measure remaining nuts)
Note the time of ingestion (check security camera footage if available)
Take a photo of the product packaging (ingredients list)
Weigh your pet (use bathroom scale: weigh yourself, then weigh yourself holding pet)

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.steps.title: Step 4: Contact Professional Help
items: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435 ($95 consultation fee may apply)
📞 Your regular vet: Call during business hours for advice
🏥 Emergency vet clinic: Go immediately if symptoms are severe

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.timeline.description: Early signs: weakness in hind legs, ataxia (wobbly gait), vomiting
Progression: tremors, reluctance to stand, abdominal pain, elevated temperature (up to 104°F/40°C)
Resolution: symptoms typically resolve with supportive care; full recovery expected

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.question: Are macadamia nuts toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.answer: Yes, macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs. The exact toxin is unknown, but even small amounts cause weakness in hind legs, vomiting, tremors, and hyperthermia. The minimum toxic dose is approximately 2.4 g/kg of body weight. Most dogs recover within 48 hours with supportive veterinary care.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.question: How many macadamia nuts are dangerous for a dog?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.answer: For a 20kg (44lb) dog, as few as 10-12 nuts can cause symptoms. Smaller dogs may react to just 2-3 nuts. The toxic threshold is approximately 0.5g of nuts per kg of body weight for mild symptoms, with severe symptoms appearing at 2.4g/kg.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.question: How long after eating macadamia nuts will my dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.answer: Symptoms typically appear within 3-12 hours after ingestion. The earliest sign is usually weakness or paralysis of the hind legs, followed by vomiting, tremors, abdominal pain, and elevated body temperature (up to 104°F/40°C).

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating macadamia nuts?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.answer: Fatalities from macadamia nut poisoning are extremely rare. The LD50 is 2.4g/kg, meaning a 20kg dog would need to eat approximately 48g of nuts (about 40-50 nuts) to reach dangerous levels. However, even sub-lethal doses cause significant discomfort and require veterinary monitoring.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate macadamia nuts?
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.faqs.answer: Do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed by a veterinarian. Induction is only effective within 30 minutes of ingestion and can cause aspiration pneumonia. Contact ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for specific guidance based on the amount consumed and time elapsed.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.vetDecision.e: Complete inability to stand or walk
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.vetDecision.u: Hind leg weakness progressing to front

emergency.ateMushrooms.riskAssessment.ro.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — do not wait

emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.title: THIS IS A TRUE EMERGENCY
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Amatoxin poisoning has a deceptive delay — your dog looks fine for 6-24 hours while the toxin destroys the liver. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.

emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.title: Collect a Mushroom Sample
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.content: If safe, collect remaining mushroom pieces (including base/bulb). Place in a paper bag (not plastic). This helps mycologists identify the species and determine toxicity risk.

emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start IV fluids. They will monitor liver enzymes for 48-72 hours. Early treatment is the ONLY effective defense.

emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.title: Prepare for Hospitalization
emergency.ateMushrooms.steps.content: If amatoxin poisoning is confirmed, treatment includes: Penicillin G, Silymarin (milk thistle), N-acetylcysteine, IV fluids, and potentially plasma transfusions. Hospitalization typically lasts 3-7 days.

emergency.ateMushrooms.timeline.description: Latent phase: dog appears normal. Toxin is being absorbed.
Gastroenteritis phase: explosive vomiting and diarrhea begin. This is the BEST treatment window.
False recovery: symptoms temporarily improve. Owners think dog is healing — FALSE sense of security.
Fulminant liver failure: jaundice, bleeding disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, death without aggressive treatment.

emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.question: Are wild mushrooms toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.answer: Many wild mushroom species are extremely toxic to dogs. The most dangerous is Amanita phalloides (Death Cap), which contains amatoxins that cause irreversible liver failure. Other toxic genera include Galerina, Lepiota, and Cortinarius. Even non-lethal species can cause severe GI upset. ANY mushroom ingestion should be treated as an emergency because you cannot reliably identify species in the field.

emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.question: How long after eating a mushroom will my dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.answer: Symptoms from amatoxin-containing mushrooms (Amanita) are DELAYED 6-24 hours. A dog appears fine initially, then develops explosive vomiting and diarrhea. After a brief "false recovery" of 12-24 hours, liver failure begins. By the time jaundice appears, damage is often irreversible. Other species cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours.

emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate a wild mushroom?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.answer: Treat EVERY wild mushroom ingestion as a life-threatening emergency. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and admit for 48-72 hour observation with liver enzyme monitoring. Do NOT wait for symptoms — early treatment is the only effective defense against amatoxin poisoning.

emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating a mushroom?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.answer: Yes. Amanita phalloides (Death Cap) has a 50-100% mortality rate in dogs without treatment. Amatoxins destroy liver cells by inhibiting RNA polymerase II. Even with treatment, mortality remains 20-30%. The lethal dose is 0.1mg/kg of amatoxin — a single Death Cap cap contains 10-15mg. Early aggressive treatment (within 12 hours) significantly improves survival.

emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.question: Can dogs eat store-bought mushrooms?
emergency.ateMushrooms.faqs.answer: Store-bought mushrooms (white button, cremini, portobello) are generally safe for dogs in small amounts. However, they offer little nutritional value and can cause GI upset if fed in large quantities or cooked with butter/oil/garlic. Never assume a field mushroom is safe — only eat mushrooms you purchased from a grocery store.

emergency.ateMushrooms.vetDecision.emerg: Bloody vomit or black tarry stool
emergency.ateMushrooms.vetDecision.urgen: Any wild mushroom ingestion in small dogs
emergency.ateMushrooms.vetDecision.monit: Small amount with no toxin risk identified

emergency.ateCookedBones.riskAssessment..action: 🚨 Vet within 1 hour — hollow bones splinter

emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.content: ⚠️ This is critical: vomiting can cause sharp bone fragments to lodge in the esophagus or puncture tissue on the way back up.

emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.title: Offer Soft Food to Cushion Fragments
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.content: Feed bread, cooked rice, or canned pumpkin to help cushion small bone fragments and reduce injury risk. This does NOT replace veterinary evaluation.

emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.title: Call Your Vet for X-Ray Assessment
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.content: Your vet will X-ray to locate bone fragments, assess obstruction risk, and determine if endoscopic or surgical removal is needed.

emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.title: Monitor Stool for 3 Days
emergency.ateCookedBones.steps.content: Watch for: bone fragments in stool (normal passage), black/tarry stool (GI bleeding), inability to defecate (obstruction), or blood. Report any abnormalities to your vet immediately.

emergency.ateCookedBones.timeline.description: Critical window: vet can induce vomiting (if advised) or perform endoscopy. Do NOT induce without professional guidance.
Fragments may cause esophageal or stomach perforation. Symptoms: drooling, reluctance to eat, pawing at mouth, vomiting.
Intestinal obstruction or perforation symptoms appear: vomiting, no bowel movement, abdominal pain, black tarry stool.
If bones passed without complications, no further action needed. If surgery was performed, recovery period.

emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.question: Why are cooked bones dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.answer: Cooked bones become brittle and splinter into sharp fragments. These shards can: (1) puncture the esophagus, stomach, or intestinal wall, (2) cause life-threatening peritonitis, (3) create intestinal obstruction, or (4) become lodged in the jaw or throat. Raw bones are safer because they are more flexible, but cooked bones are NEVER safe.

emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.question: What are the symptoms if my dog ate cooked bones?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.answer: Symptoms of bone-related injury include: vomiting (possibly bloody), diarrhea (may contain blood or look black/tarry), abdominal pain (hunched posture, reluctance to move), difficulty defecating, excessive drooling, pawing at mouth, and lethargy. Symptoms may appear within hours or be delayed 1-3 days if a slow obstruction develops.

emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate cooked bones?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.answer: Do NOT induce vomiting if your dog ate cooked bones. Regurgitating sharp bone fragments can cause additional damage to the esophagus or become lodged in the throat. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 for immediate guidance.

emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.question: What is the treatment for bone ingestion in dogs?
emergency.ateCookedBones.faqs.answer: Treatment depends on severity: (1) If bone is lodged in throat/mouth — manual removal under sedation. (2) If bone is in stomach — endoscopic retrieval. (3) If obstruction or perforation — emergency surgery. (4) If small, softened pieces — monitoring with bread/bulk diet to cushion passage. X-rays or ultrasound determine the approach.

emergency.ateCookedBones.vetDecision.eme: Inability to defecate with abdominal pain
emergency.ateCookedBones.vetDecision.urg: Excessive drooling or pawing at mouth

emergency.atePlastic.steps.title: Assess the Ingested Object
emergency.atePlastic.steps.content: If possible, find the remaining pieces and measure them. Was it a wrapper, toy piece, or bag? Size and shape determine risk.

emergency.atePlastic.steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Large or Sharp
emergency.atePlastic.steps.content: ⚠️ Large objects can lodge in the esophagus; sharp edges can cause damage during regurgitation. Only induce if instructed by a vet for small, smooth items within 30 minutes of ingestion.

emergency.atePlastic.steps.title: Feed a Bulk Meal
emergency.atePlastic.steps.content: Offer bread, canned pumpkin, or cooked rice to help wrap the plastic and encourage safe passage. This is NOT a substitute for veterinary care if the object is large.

emergency.atePlastic.steps.title: Monitor Closely for 48 Hours
emergency.atePlastic.steps.content: Check: Is your dog eating? Vomiting? Defecating? Locate the plastic in stool if possible. Absence of bowel movement for 24+ hours with vomiting = emergency.

emergency.atePlastic.timeline.description: Assess the object. If small (<2cm), monitor. If large or sharp, call vet immediately.
Small pieces may pass through stomach. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, or abdominal pain.
Critical monitoring window. If no bowel movement AND vomiting = possible obstruction. Seek emergency care.
If still no bowel movement, X-ray needed to locate blockage. Surgery may be required if object is lodged.

emergency.atePlastic.faqs.question: Is plastic dangerous for dogs?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs.answer: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause life-threatening intestinal obstruction. The danger depends on the size and shape of the plastic object relative to your dog. Items larger than 2cm wide are unlikely to pass through the pylorus (stomach exit) or ileocecal junction. Sharp plastic edges can also cause GI perforation.

emergency.atePlastic.faqs.question: Symptoms of plastic blockage in dogs?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 2-48 hours: repeated vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, lethargy, abdominal pain, absence of bowel movements, and dehydration. A complete obstruction causes persistent vomiting, dehydration, and shock within 24-72 hours. This is a surgical emergency.

emergency.atePlastic.faqs.question: How long does it take for plastic to pass through a dog?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs.answer: Small plastic pieces (under 2cm) typically pass through the GI tract within 24-48 hours and appear in stool. Larger items may take 3-5 days or become lodged. If plastic has not passed within 48 hours, or if vomiting occurs, veterinary intervention is required.

emergency.atePlastic.faqs.question: When should I call the vet if my dog ate plastic?
emergency.atePlastic.faqs.answer: Call your vet immediately if: (1) the plastic object is larger than 2cm in any dimension, (2) your dog vomits more than once, (3) no bowel movement occurs within 48 hours, (4) your dog shows abdominal pain or lethargy, or (5) the plastic piece is sharp/rigid. Do NOT wait for symptoms if the object is large.

emergency.atePlastic.vetDecision.emergen: Persistent vomiting with no bowel movement
emergency.atePlastic.vetDecision.urgent: Object 2-3cm and not seen in stool after 24h

emergency.ateMedication.riskAssessment.r.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — GI ulcers, kidney failure

emergency.ateMedication.steps.title: Gather All Medication Information
emergency.ateMedication.steps.content: Bring the pill bottle: drug name, strength (mg), number of pills missing. Calculate total mg consumed: strength × pills. This is critical for toxicity assessment.

emergency.ateMedication.steps.title: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
emergency.ateMedication.steps.content: ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — some medications cause delayed toxicity.

emergency.ateMedication.steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Professional Guidance
emergency.ateMedication.steps.content: Some medications are rapidly absorbed; others can cause seizures if vomited. Only induce if ASPCA or your vet instructs you to.

emergency.ateMedication.steps.title: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateMedication.steps.content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if early), administer activated charcoal, and begin IV fluids. Blood work will monitor liver/kidney function for 24-72 hours.

emergency.ateMedication.timeline.description: Best window for induced vomiting. Call poison control before inducing.
Drug absorption phase. Symptoms begin for fast-acting drugs (ibuprofen): vomiting, abdominal pain.
GI ulceration phase (NSAIDs). Symptoms: bloody vomiting, black tarry stool, kidney stress begins.
Organ damage phase: liver failure (acetaminophen), kidney failure (NSAIDs), seizures (antidepressants). Hospitalization required.

emergency.ateMedication.faqs.question: Which human medications are most toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs.answer: The most dangerous human medications for dogs include: (1) NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) — GI ulcers and kidney failure at 50mg/kg. (2) Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — liver damage and methemoglobinemia at 75mg/kg. (3) Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs) — serotonin syndrome. (4) ADHD medications (amphetamines) — severe stimulation. (5) Benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation. (6) Vitamin D supplements — fatal hypercalcemia.

emergency.ateMedication.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of ibuprofen poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 1-4 hours: vomiting (possibly with blood), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. At toxic doses (50mg/kg+): kidney failure (increased thirst/urination, then decreased urine), GI ulceration, liver damage, and seizures. Megaesophagus (enlarged esophagus) can occur with chronic exposure. Treatment includes activated charcoal, gastroprotectants, IV fluids, and blood monitoring.

emergency.ateMedication.faqs.question: Should I induce vomiting if my dog ate medication?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs.answer: Inducing vomiting may be recommended if ingestion occurred within 30 minutes and your dog is alert. However, do NOT induce vomiting for: caustic substances, if your dog is already symptomatic (seizures, ataxia), or if the medication is rapidly absorbed. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 with the drug name, strength, and estimated number of pills consumed.

emergency.ateMedication.faqs.question: How is medication toxicity treated in dogs?
emergency.ateMedication.faqs.answer: Treatment depends on the drug: (1) Induced vomiting + activated charcoal (if early), (2) IV fluids for elimination, (3) Gastroprotectants (omeprazole, sucralfate) for NSAIDs, (4) N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen, (5) Cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, (6) Lipid emulsion therapy for fat-soluble drugs. Hospitalization for 24-72 hours is typical for significant ingestions.

emergency.ateMedication.vetDecision.emer: Any amount of: antidepressant overdose, ADHD medication, insulin, or heart medications
Vomiting, tremors, or seizures after ingestion
More than 2-3x the toxic dose of any medication
emergency.ateMedication.vetDecision.urge: Small dose (1-2 pills) of ibuprofen or acetaminophen
Any dose of vitamin D, calcium, or iron supplements
Dog alert but consumed unknown pills
emergency.ateMedication.vetDecision.moni: Single small pill at sub-toxic dose
No symptoms within 4 hours of small ingestion
Topical medication licked off skin (small amount)
Confirmed non-toxic supplement (B vitamins in small amounts)

emergency.ateRodenticide.riskAssessment..action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — internal bleeding delayed
🚨 Emergency vet NOW — seizures within hours

emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.title: Step 1: This Is a Dire Emergency
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.content: Do NOT wait for symptoms. Anticoagulant rodenticides have a 2-5 day delay before bleeding begins. By the time symptoms appear, the damage is done. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 NOW.

emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.title: Step 2: Bring the Product Package
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.content: Take the bait package or a photo to the vet. The active ingredient determines treatment: anticoagulants need Vitamin K1; bromethalin needs brain swelling management; cholecalciferol needs calcium-lowering therapy.

emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.title: Step 3: Go to Emergency Vet for Decontamination
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.content: Your vet will induce vomiting (if within 1-2 hours), administer activated charcoal, and start specific antidotes. For anticoagulants: Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks with blood clotting tests.

emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.title: Step 4: Hospitalization May Be Required
emergency.ateRodenticide.steps.content: Bromethalin poisoning requires 24-72 hour monitoring with mannitol for brain swelling. Anticoagulant cases need plasma transfusions if bleeding is active. Early treatment dramatically improves survival.

emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.question: Is rat poison deadly to dogs?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.answer: Yes, rat poison (rodenticide) is one of the most deadly toxins for dogs. There are two main types: (1) Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, bromadiolone, brodifacoum) — prevent blood clotting, causing fatal internal bleeding. Single-dose types require one feeding; multiple-dose types are cumulative. (2) Neurotoxic rodenticides (bromethalin, strychnine, cholecalciferol) — cause brain swelling, seizures, or hypercalcium within hours. Without treatment, mortality rates are 50-90%.

emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of rat poison in dogs?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.answer: Anticoagulant symptoms appear 2-5 days after ingestion: weakness, pale gums, coughing blood, bloody vomit/diarrhea, nosebleeds, and collapse. Neurotoxic (bromethalin) symptoms appear within 2-24 hours: severe muscle tremors, seizures, ataxia, and paralysis. Cholecalciferol causes kidney failure with increased thirst/urination within 12-36 hours.

emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.question: Can my dog survive rat poison?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. Anticoagulant poisoning is treatable with Vitamin K1 for 4-6 weeks; survival rate is 80-90% if treated before symptoms appear. Bromethalin has no antidote — treatment is supportive care (activated charcoal, mannitol for brain swelling) with 50-70% survival if treated early. Strychnine and cholecalciferol also require immediate veterinary intervention.

emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate rat poison?
emergency.ateRodenticide.faqs.answer: Treat this as a dire emergency: (1) Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. (2) Go to the nearest emergency vet NOW — do not wait for symptoms. (3) Bring the product label to identify the active ingredient. (4) Induced vomiting within 1-2 hours may help prevent absorption. (5) Even if your dog seems fine, delayed symptoms are common and early treatment is life-saving.

emergency.ateTobacco.steps.title: Step 1: Calculate Total Nicotine
emergency.ateTobacco.steps.content: Count cigarettes/packages consumed. Cigarette: 10-15mg each. E-liquid: check mg/mL concentration × mL consumed. This determines toxicity risk.

emergency.ateTobacco.steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control IMMEDIATELY
emergency.ateTobacco.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Nicotine is absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa — effects can begin within 15 minutes.

emergency.ateTobacco.steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting If Symptomatic
emergency.ateTobacco.steps.content: ⚠️ If your dog shows tremors, seizures, or agitation, inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only induce if instructed by a professional AND your dog is asymptomatic within 15 minutes.

emergency.ateTobacco.steps.title: Step 4: Go to Emergency Vet for Monitoring
emergency.ateTobacco.steps.content: Your vet will administer activated charcoal, provide IV fluids, and monitor heart rhythm and respiratory function. Symptoms can progress rapidly.

emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.question: How much nicotine is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.answer: The toxic dose of nicotine in dogs is 20-100mg/kg. For a 20kg dog, this equals 400-2000mg of nicotine. Sources: 1 cigarette = 10-15mg nicotine, 1 cigarette butt = 5-7mg, nicotine patch = 8-21mg, nicotine gum = 2-4mg, e-liquid = 3-24mg/mL (highly concentrated). Even ONE cigarette can cause symptoms in a small dog.

emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of nicotine poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 15-60 minutes: hypersalivation, vomiting, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), muscle tremors, agitation, and hypertension. As toxicity progresses: bradycardia (slow heart rate), weakness, collapse, respiratory paralysis, and seizures. The biphasic effect — first excitation then depression — is characteristic of nicotine poisoning.

emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.question: Is vape liquid dangerous for dogs?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.answer: Yes, e-liquid (vape juice) is EXTREMELY dangerous due to high nicotine concentration. A single 10mL bottle can contain 30-240mg of nicotine — enough to kill multiple small dogs. The sweet flavorings also attract dogs. Ingestion of even small amounts requires emergency veterinary treatment.

emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.question: What should I do if my dog ate tobacco?
emergency.ateTobacco.faqs.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately. Calculate total nicotine consumed: mg per item × number of items. Go to emergency vet if your dog ingested: (1) more than 1 cigarette, (2) any e-liquid, (3) a nicotine patch, or (4) any amount if your dog shows symptoms. Do NOT induce vomiting if seizures or tremors are present.

emergency.ateMarijuana.riskAssessment.ro.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — high THC + chocolate
📞 May also contain xylitol — call vet

emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.title: Step 1: Remove All Remaining Product
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.content: Check for packaging — note THC content in mg per piece and total pieces eaten. This determines toxicity risk.

emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.title: Step 2: Check for Xylitol (CBD Products)
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.content: ⚠️ Some CBD oils contain xylitol, which is extremely toxic to dogs. Check the ingredient list immediately.

emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.title: Step 3: Call Poison Control or Vet
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Be honest — they will provide guidance without judgment.

emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.title: Step 4: Monitor Symptoms
emergency.ateMarijuana.steps.content: Watch for: stumbling, dilated pupils, urinary incontinence, drooling, slow heart rate, hypothermia. Severe cases: seizures or coma. Symptoms can last 12-72 hours.

emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.question: Is marijuana toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.answer: Yes, THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) is toxic to dogs. Dogs have more cannabinoid receptors (CB1) in the brain than humans, making them significantly more sensitive. Edibles (gummies, brownies, cookies) are especially dangerous due to high THC concentration — one gummy can contain 10-100mg THC, which is toxic to most dogs.

emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of marijuana poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 30-90 minutes: dazed appearance, stumbling/ataxia, urinary incontinence (dripping urine), drooling, dilated pupils, vomiting, tremors, bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypothermia, and in severe cases: seizures or coma. Be honest with your vet — marijuana toxicosis is rarely fatal, and honesty ensures proper treatment.

emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.question: Are marijuana edibles more dangerous than dried cannabis?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.answer: Yes, edibles are significantly more dangerous: (1) High THC concentration (10-100mg per piece), (2) Often contain chocolate (double toxicity), (3) Faster absorption from GI tract, (4) Dogs eat multiple pieces quickly. Edibles account for the majority of severe cannabis toxicosis cases in dogs.

emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating marijuana?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.answer: Fatalities from marijuana alone are rare in dogs — the LD50 is very high (over 3g/kg of THC). However, edibles pose additional risks: chocolate toxicity, xylitol in some CBD products, and overdose from multiple ingestion. Death is more likely from complications (aspiration pneumonia, hypothermia) or combined toxins. Always seek veterinary care.

emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.question: Should I tell my vet my dog ate marijuana?
emergency.ateMarijuana.faqs.answer: Yes, always be honest. Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Knowing your dog ate marijuana ensures they provide appropriate care: inducing vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, IV fluids, thermoregulation, and monitoring heart rate. Without this information, your dog may undergo unnecessary tests or receive inappropriate treatment.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.riskAssessment.r.action: 🚨 Emergency vet NOW — liver failure too

emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.title: Step 1: Calculate Total Xylitol Consumed
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.content: Find the packaging. Xylitol content is listed in grams per piece. Calculate: grams per piece × pieces eaten. This determines whether hypoglycemia risk (0.1g/kg) or liver failure risk (0.5g/kg) threshold is crossed.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control and Go to Emergency Vet
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Do NOT wait for symptoms — hypoglycemia can cause death within hours. Xylitol is absorbed rapidly.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.content: ⚠️ If instructed to induce at home, use hydrogen peroxide (1 tsp per 5lbs). But go to vet ASAP — xylitol may need IV dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.title: Step 4: Prepare for Hospitalization
emergency.ateXylitolGum.steps.content: Your vet will: induce vomiting (if early), give activated charcoal, start IV dextrose, and monitor blood glucose for 24 hours. Liver enzymes will be checked for 72 hours. Early treatment has 80%+ survival.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.answer: Xylitol is toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1g/kg for hypoglycemia and 0.5g/kg for liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1.0g of xylitol — meaning ONE piece can cause severe hypoglycemia in a small-to-medium dog. Emergency treatment is needed even for tiny amounts.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of xylitol poisoning in dogs?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear within 10-60 minutes (sometimes delayed 12 hours): vomiting, lethargy, weakness, collapse, tremors, seizures, and coma — these result from hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Liver failure symptoms (jaundice, coagulopathy) may be delayed 12-72 hours. Even small amounts cause dangerously low blood sugar.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.question: Why is xylitol toxic to dogs but not humans?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.answer: In dogs, xylitol is rapidly absorbed and triggers a massive insulin release from the pancreas — 6-7x more than glucose would. This causes profound hypoglycemia. Humans do not have this insulin response. Additionally, xylitol causes dose-dependent hepatocellular necrosis in dogs through mechanisms not seen in humans.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.question: What products contain xylitol?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.answer: Xylitol is found in: sugar-free gum, mints, peanut butter (some brands), toothpaste, mouthwash, nasal sprays, chewable vitamins, baked goods, ice cream, and "birch sugar" sold as a sweetener. Some brands: Trident, Orbit, Ice Breakers, Eclipse. Always check ingredient lists before giving human food to dogs.

emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.question: Can a dog survive xylitol poisoning?
emergency.ateXylitolGum.faqs.answer: Yes, with immediate treatment. If caught within 30 minutes, induced vomiting prevents absorption. If hypoglycemia has begun, IV dextrose corrects blood sugar. Even with liver damage, aggressive hospital care (IV fluids, liver protectants, plasma transfusions) has 70-80% survival if treatment begins within 8 hours. Delayed treatment has worse prognosis.

emergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Call for Help Immediately
emergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Contact ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your nearest emergency vet. Time is critical — do not wait for symptoms to appear.

emergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Gather Information
emergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Note the type of chocolate (milk, dark, baking), estimated amount consumed, and your dog's weight. This helps the vet assess toxicity risk.

emergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
emergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Inducing vomiting can cause aspiration pneumonia or worsen the situation. Only do so if explicitly instructed by a veterinarian.

emergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Monitor Symptoms Closely
emergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Watch for vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, increased thirst, rapid breathing, and seizures. Symptoms may appear within 2-4 hours.

emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: How much chocolate is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Toxicity depends on the type of chocolate and your dog's weight. Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate is 2-3x more toxic. Baking chocolate is the most dangerous — as little as 0.1 oz per pound can be lethal. Use our toxicity calculator to assess your dog's specific risk.

emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: How long after eating chocolate will a dog show symptoms?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Symptoms typically appear within 2-4 hours but can be delayed up to 12 hours. Early signs include vomiting, diarrhea, and restlessness. Severe symptoms (seizures, irregular heartbeat) may appear 6-12 hours after ingestion. Theobromine is absorbed slowly, so symptoms can worsen over time.

emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: Can a dog die from eating chocolate?
emergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Yes, chocolate can be fatal to dogs. The lethal dose of theobromine is approximately 100-500 mg per kg of body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals roughly 200g of milk chocolate or 100g of dark chocolate. Immediate veterinary treatment significantly improves survival rates.

emergency.ateGrapes.steps.title: Call Your Vet Immediately
emergency.ateGrapes.steps.content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 right away. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.

emergency.ateGrapes.steps.title: Note the Amount
emergency.ateGrapes.steps.content: Record how many grapes or raisins your dog ate and their weight. This helps determine toxicity risk.

emergency.ateGrapes.steps.title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateGrapes.steps.content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting or administer activated charcoal to prevent absorption.

emergency.ateGrapes.steps.title: Monitor for 72 Hours
emergency.ateGrapes.steps.content: Kidney damage may not show symptoms immediately. Watch for vomiting, lethargy, decreased urination, and loss of appetite.

emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.question: How many grapes are toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.answer: The toxic dose is not established, but as few as 1-2 grapes can cause kidney failure in some dogs. Raisins are more concentrated and thus more dangerous. There is no known safe amount — any ingestion should be treated as an emergency.

emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.question: How long after eating grapes do symptoms appear?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.answer: Vomiting and diarrhea typically begin within 6-12 hours. Signs of kidney failure (decreased urination, lethargy, loss of appetite) may not appear until 24-72 hours after ingestion. Early veterinary intervention is critical.

emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.question: Why are grapes toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateGrapes.faqs.answer: The exact toxic mechanism is still unknown. Tartaric acid is the suspected toxin, with varying concentrations between grape varieties. This unpredictability makes any grape ingestion potentially dangerous.

emergency.ateXylitol.steps.title: Call Your Vet NOW
emergency.ateXylitol.steps.content: Xylitol acts fast. Contact your vet or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 immediately — do not wait for symptoms.

emergency.ateXylitol.steps.title: Check the Product Label
emergency.ateXylitol.steps.content: Find the xylitol content (in grams) and calculate your dog's exposure. Note: it may be listed as 'birch sugar.'

emergency.ateXylitol.steps.title: Go to the Vet Immediately
emergency.ateXylitol.steps.content: Your vet will likely induce vomiting (if within 1 hour), start IV dextrose, and monitor liver enzymes for 72 hours.

emergency.ateXylitol.steps.title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
emergency.ateXylitol.steps.content: By the time symptoms appear (vomiting, lethargy, seizures), treatment may be less effective. Early intervention saves lives.

emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.question: How much xylitol is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.answer: As little as 0.1g of xylitol per kg of body weight can cause hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). Doses above 0.5g/kg can cause acute liver failure. A single piece of sugar-free gum can contain 0.3-1g of xylitol — potentially lethal for a small dog.

emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.question: How fast does xylitol affect dogs?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.answer: Hypoglycemia can develop within 10-30 minutes of ingestion. Liver damage may take 8-12 hours to manifest. Rapid treatment is essential — do not wait for symptoms.

emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.question: Where is xylitol found?
emergency.ateXylitol.faqs.answer: Xylitol is found in sugar-free gum, candy, baked goods, peanut butter, toothpaste, mouthwash, and some medications. Always check labels — it may be listed as 'birch sugar' or 'xylitol'.

emergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Call Your Vet
emergency.ateOnion.steps.content: Contact your veterinarian or ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435. Note the amount and type of onion consumed.

emergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Vet May Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateOnion.steps.content: If ingestion was recent (within 2 hours), your vet may induce vomiting to prevent further absorption of thiosulfate compounds.

emergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Monitor for Anemia Symptoms
emergency.ateOnion.steps.content: Watch for weakness, pale gums, rapid breathing, and reddish-brown urine over the next 1-3 days.

emergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Blood Work May Be Needed
emergency.ateOnion.steps.content: Your vet may recommend a CBC blood test to check for Heinz body anemia, which confirms onion toxicity.

emergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: How much onion is toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Onion toxicity occurs at approximately 0.5% of the dog's body weight. For a 20kg (44lb) dog, this equals about 100g (3.5oz) of onion. All forms are toxic: raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated. Onion powder is especially concentrated and dangerous.

emergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: How long after eating onion do symptoms appear?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Symptoms typically develop 1-3 days after ingestion as red blood cells are progressively destroyed. Early signs include weakness, pale gums, and reddish urine. Severe cases can lead to collapse and require blood transfusion.

emergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: Are all onion types toxic to dogs?
emergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Yes — all Allium species are toxic: onions, garlic, leeks, chives, and shallots. Garlic is less toxic per gram but still dangerous in quantity. Cooking does not reduce toxicity. Onion powder is the most concentrated form.

emergency.ateSock.steps.title: Call Your Vet Immediately
emergency.ateSock.steps.content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the sock was eaten and your dog's size — this determines urgency.

emergency.ateSock.steps.title: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
emergency.ateSock.steps.content: Unlike toxins, foreign objects can cause more damage coming back up. Only induce vomiting if your vet explicitly instructs you to.

emergency.ateSock.steps.title: Vet May Retrieve Endoscopically
emergency.ateSock.steps.content: If the sock is still in the stomach (within 12-24 hours), your vet may remove it via endoscopy — a non-surgical procedure using a camera and grabber.

emergency.ateSock.steps.title: Monitor for Blockage Signs
emergency.ateSock.steps.content: Watch for vomiting after eating, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.

emergency.ateSock.faqs.question: Will my dog pass a sock naturally?
emergency.ateSock.faqs.answer: Small socks may pass through the digestive tract within 24-48 hours, but this is not guaranteed. Larger socks or those that become lodged can cause life-threatening intestinal blockage. Never wait to see if it passes — consult your vet immediately.

emergency.ateSock.faqs.question: How long after eating a sock will symptoms appear?
emergency.ateSock.faqs.answer: Symptoms of intestinal blockage typically appear within 2-24 hours. Watch for vomiting (especially after eating), loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and inability to defecate. These are emergency signs.

emergency.ateSock.faqs.question: What is the treatment for sock ingestion?
emergency.ateSock.faqs.answer: Treatment depends on location and size. Your vet may induce vomiting (if within 2 hours), perform endoscopy to retrieve the object, or conduct abdominal surgery if the sock has caused a blockage. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.title: EMERGENCY VET NOW
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Every minute counts.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.title: Do NOT Wait for Symptoms
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.content: By the time symptoms appear, kidney damage may be irreversible. The antidote must be given within 8-12 hours to be effective.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.title: Bring the Container
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.content: Take the antifreeze container to the vet. This confirms the active ingredient (ethylene glycol) and concentration.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.title: Treatment Window is Critical
emergency.ateAntifreeze.steps.content: Your vet will administer fomepizole (4-MP) or ethanol IV to block metabolism. After 12 hours, treatment is much less effective.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.question: How much antifreeze is lethal to dogs?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.answer: As little as 1 teaspoon (5ml) of antifreeze can kill a 10lb (4.5kg) dog. The lethal dose of ethylene glycol is approximately 4.4ml per kg of body weight. This makes antifreeze one of the most dangerous household toxins for pets.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.question: How fast does antifreeze kill dogs?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.answer: Without treatment, antifreeze is fatal within 12-36 hours. The antidote (fomepizole or ethanol) must be administered within 8-12 hours of ingestion to be effective. After kidney failure begins, survival rates drop dramatically.

emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of antifreeze poisoning?
emergency.ateAntifreeze.faqs.answer: Stage 1 (30 min-12 hrs): drunken behavior, vomiting, seizures. Stage 2 (12-24 hrs): apparent improvement (misleading). Stage 3 (24-72 hrs): kidney failure, severe lethargy, mouth ulcers, coma. Early treatment is critical.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Step 1: Remove All Chocolate Immediately
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Cats are naturally curious but also more sensitive to toxins. Remove any remaining chocolate from their environment.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control or Vet
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Cats are more sensitive to theobromine than dogs — small amounts are concerning.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Without Vet Approval
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: ⚠️ Cats may hide symptoms until severe. Inducing vomiting risks aspiration. Only do so if instructed by a veterinarian.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.title: Step 4: Go to Vet for Cardiac Monitoring
catEmergency.ateChocolate.steps.content: Your vet may recommend induced vomiting (if early), activated charcoal, and ECG monitoring to watch for arrhythmias.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: Is chocolate toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Yes, chocolate is toxic to cats — often more so than to dogs relative to body weight. Cats are more sensitive to theobromine because they metabolize it more slowly. The same toxic principle applies: theobromine and caffeine cause CNS stimulation, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially seizures.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: Why are cats more sensitive than dogs?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Cats have lower activity of cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for metabolizing theobromine. While dogs take 17+ hours to clear theobromine, cats may take even longer. Additionally, cats typically weigh less (4-6kg average), so the dose-per-kg ratio from the same amount of chocolate is higher.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: How much chocolate is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Milk chocolate becomes toxic at approximately 0.5 oz per pound of body weight. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are 2-5x more toxic. For a 5kg (11lb) cat, as little as 20g of milk chocolate (about half a standard bar) can cause symptoms. Baking chocolate is lethal at 5-10g for an average cat.

catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.question: What should I do if my cat ate chocolate?
catEmergency.ateChocolate.faqs.answer: Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or your vet immediately. Cats are more sensitive than dogs — even small amounts are concerning. Bring the chocolate packaging to identify theobromine content. Do NOT wait for symptoms, as cardiac arrhythmias can be sudden and fatal.

catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Step 1: Note the Type and Amount
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.content: Was it raw onion, cooked onion, onion powder, or a product containing onion? Powder is most concentrated. Calculate approximate amount.

catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Step 2: Call Vet or Poison Control
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Even small amounts can cause delayed anemia — early blood work may be needed.

catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Step 3: Do NOT Induce Vomiting Unless Instructed
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.content: ⚠️ Symptoms are delayed 1-5 days. Induction is not effective after absorption. Your vet may induce vomiting if ingestion was very recent.

catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.title: Step 4: Schedule Blood Work
catEmergency.ateOnion.steps.content: Your vet will check for Heinz bodies and monitor red blood cell count for 3-5 days. Early detection of anemia allows transfusion if needed.

catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: Are onions toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Yes, onions are highly toxic to cats — more so than dogs relative to body weight. Onions contain N-propyl disulfide and thiosulfates that cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, leading to Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Cats are uniquely vulnerable because their hemoglobin is more susceptible to oxidation, and they produce methemoglobin more readily.

catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: How much onion is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Even small amounts are dangerous. Toxic effects can occur at 5g/kg body weight (about 1 tablespoon for a 4kg cat). Regular consumption of smaller amounts (even trace amounts in baby food or broth) can cause cumulative damage. Raw, cooked, powdered, and dehydrated onions are all toxic.

catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of onion poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Symptoms appear 1-5 days after ingestion: pale or yellow gums (anemia/jaundice), weakness, rapid breathing, reddish-brown urine (hemoglobinuria), vomiting, and lethargy. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear showing damaged red blood cells. Severe cases require blood transfusion.

catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.question: Can onion powder hurt cats?
catEmergency.ateOnion.faqs.answer: Yes, onion powder is concentrated and especially dangerous. Even small amounts in broth, gravy, baby food, or treats can cause toxicity. Many commercial products contain hidden onion or garlic powder. Always check ingredient labels before sharing human food with cats.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.title: Step 1: Remove All Garlic Immediately
catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.content: Remove any remaining garlic, garlic-containing foods, or supplements from your cat's reach.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.title: Step 2: Call Poison Control
catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Garlic is more toxic than onion — small amounts require professional guidance.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.title: Step 3: Schedule Blood Work for Days 3-5
catEmergency.ateGarlic.steps.content: Anemia peaks 3-5 days after ingestion. Even if your cat seems fine, delayed Heinz body anemia can be life-threatening.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.question: Is garlic toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.answer: Yes, garlic is highly toxic to cats — approximately 5x more potent than onion per gram. Garlic (Allium sativum) contains allicin, alliin, and allyl propyl disulfide, which cause severe oxidative damage to feline red blood cells. Cats are uniquely susceptible due to the structure of their hemoglobin molecule.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.question: How much garlic is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.answer: As little as 5g of garlic per kg of body weight can cause toxicity. For a 4kg cat, this equals just 1 small clove (approximately 5g). Toxic effects can also occur from chronic low-dose exposure — even trace amounts in food or supplements over weeks can accumulate and cause anemia.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.question: Is garlic salt/powder dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.answer: Yes, garlic powder and salt are concentrated forms. As little as 1/8 teaspoon of garlic powder can be toxic to a small cat. Dry garlic powder, garlic supplements, garlic-flavored treats, and garlic-infused oils all pose risks. Many human foods contain hidden garlic — always check labels.

catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of garlic poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateGarlic.faqs.answer: Symptoms develop 1-5 days after ingestion: pale gums (anemia), lethargy, weakness, rapid breathing, elevated heart rate, jaundice (yellow gums/eyes), reddish-brown urine, vomiting, and collapse. Heinz body anemia is confirmed by blood smear. Severe cases require blood transfusions.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.title: Step 1: Wash Your Cat If Oil Is On Fur/Skin
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.content: Use Dawn dish soap (cuts oil) to wash off any topical exposure. Rinse thoroughly. Do NOT use water alone — oil repels water.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.title: Step 2: Remove From Exposure Source
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.content: Turn off diffusers, remove oil containers, and ventilate the area. Move your cat to fresh air.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.title: Step 3: Call Poison Control
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.content: 📞 ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. Bring the oil bottle — tell them the botanical name and phenol/terpene content if listed.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.title: Step 4: Do NOT Induce Vomiting
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.steps.content: ⚠️ Essential oils have high aspiration pneumonia risk. Vomiting can cause oil to enter lungs. Go to vet for safe decontamination.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.question: Why are essential oils toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.answer: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzymes needed to metabolize certain compounds in essential oils (terpenes, phenols, ketones). This makes them 10x more sensitive than dogs to tea tree oil, citrus oils, eucalyptus, peppermint, and pine oils. Even topical application on skin can cause toxicity if the cat licks it off.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.question: Which essential oils are most dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.answer: Most dangerous: Tea tree (melaleuca), wintergreen, peppermint, pine, eucalyptus, citrus (limonene, linalool), cinnamon, clove, ylang ylang, birch, and thyme. Tea tree oil is most commonly reported — even 10-20mL on skin can be fatal. Diffusers are also dangerous as cats inhale droplets and groom them from fur.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of essential oil poisoning in cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.answer: Symptoms depend on oil type and route: (1) Ingestion: drooling, vomiting, tremors, ataxia, weakness, hypothermia. (2) Skin absorption: lethargy, hypersalivation, liver damage. (3) Inhalation: respiratory distress, aspiration pneumonia. Tea tree oil specifically causes severe hypothermia and ataxia within 2-8 hours.

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.question: Are essential oil diffusers dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.faqs.answer: Yes, diffusers pose three risks: (1) Inhaled droplets settle on fur and are groomed off, causing ingestion. (2) Volatilized oils irritate feline respiratory passages (cats have efficient smell but sensitive airways). (3) Concentrated oil in the diffuser water can be spilled and licked. Use diffusers only in well-ventilated rooms your cat cannot access.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.criticalWarn: NEVER pull on string protruding from your cat. The line may be anchored internally — pulling can cut through the intestine.
ALWAYS check under your cat's tongue. Fishing line frequently anchors at the base of the tongue.
This requires emergency surgery — do not wait for symptoms.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.riskAssessme.action: 🚨 DO NOT PULL — Emergency vet NOW

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.title: Step 1: Check Under Your Cat's Tongue
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.content: Gently open your mouth and look under the tongue and at the base. Fishing line commonly anchors here. If you see string — do NOT pull.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.title: Step 2: Do NOT Pull Any Protruding String
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.content: ⚠️ Pulling can cause the line to saw through the intestinal wall. Leave it alone and go to emergency vet.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.title: Step 3: Go to Emergency Vet for X-rays/Surgery
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.content: Linear foreign bodies often require surgical removal. Your vet will take X-rays, start IV fluids, and perform enterotomy to remove the line.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.title: Step 4: Prepare for Hospitalization
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.steps.content: Post-surgery, your cat will need 2-5 days hospitalization for IV antibiotics, pain management, and monitoring for anastomotic leakage.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.question: Why is fishing line so dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.answer: Fishing line is a linear foreign body — when swallowed, it anchors at one end (under tongue, in stomach, or at pylorus) while the rest extends through the intestines. Peristalsis pulls the line taut, causing the intestine to accordion-pleat around it. The line then saws through the intestinal wall, causing multiple perforations, peritonitis, and death if not surgically removed.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of linear foreign body in cats?
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.answer: Symptoms include: string visible under tongue or protruding from anus, vomiting (especially after eating), drooling, difficulty swallowing, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, and fever. CRITICAL: Always check under the tongue and around the base of the tongue — the line may be anchored there.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.question: Should I pull the string out of my cat?
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.answer: NO! Never pull on a string or line protruding from your cat mouth or anus. The line may be anchored internally — pulling it can saw through the intestinal wall causing perforations. Go to emergency vet immediately for proper removal under anesthesia.

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.question: What is the treatment for fishing line ingestion in cats?
catEmergency.ateFishingLine.faqs.answer: Treatment requires emergency surgery (enterotomy or gastrotomy) to remove the line. Multiple incisions may be needed along the intestine to release the plicated segments. IV antibiotics treat peritonitis, and fluids correct dehydration. Prognosis depends on how many perforations occurred — early surgery has 80-90% survival; delayed treatment with multiple perforations has 50-60% survival.

catEmergency.ateLily.steps.title: Step 1: EMERGENCY VET NOW
catEmergency.ateLily.steps.content: Go to the nearest emergency vet immediately. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 en route. Time is critical.

catEmergency.ateLily.steps.title: Step 2: Bring a Plant Sample
catEmergency.ateLily.steps.content: Take the lily plant or a photo to the vet. This confirms the species and helps assess toxicity risk.

catEmergency.ateLily.steps.title: Step 3: IV Fluids Are Critical
catEmergency.ateLily.steps.content: Your vet will start aggressive IV fluid therapy to protect the kidneys. This must begin within 18 hours of ingestion for best outcomes.

catEmergency.ateLily.steps.title: Step 4: Activated Charcoal May Help
catEmergency.ateLily.steps.content: If ingestion was recent, your vet may administer activated charcoal to absorb remaining toxins in the GI tract.

catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.question: Which lilies are toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.answer: True lilies (Lilium spp.) and Hemerocallis (daylilies) are highly toxic: Easter lily, Tiger lily, Asiatic lily, Oriental lily, Stargazer lily. Even pollen, leaves, or water from the vase can cause kidney failure. Not toxic: Peace lily, Lily of the Valley (different toxin), Calla lily.

catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.question: How much lily is toxic to cats?
catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.answer: Ingestion of as little as 2-3 petals or leaves, or exposure to pollen (grooming pollen off fur), can cause acute kidney failure. There is no safe amount — any exposure requires emergency veterinary treatment.

catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.question: How long after lily ingestion do symptoms appear?
catEmergency.ateLily.faqs.answer: Vomiting and lethargy begin within 1-6 hours. Kidney damage is detectable within 12-24 hours. Without treatment, kidney failure develops within 24-72 hours and is often fatal. Early IV fluid therapy is critical.

catEmergency.ateString.steps.title: Step 1: Call Your Vet Immediately
catEmergency.ateString.steps.content: Contact your veterinarian right away. Note when the string was eaten and how much.

catEmergency.ateString.steps.title: Step 2: DO NOT Pull Visible String
catEmergency.ateString.steps.content: If string is hanging from the mouth or anus, do NOT pull it. This can cause the anchored end to cut through intestinal tissue.

catEmergency.ateString.steps.title: Step 3: Check Under the Tongue
catEmergency.ateString.steps.content: If safe to do so, check if string is wrapped around the base of the tongue. If so, this is an emergency — go to the vet NOW.

catEmergency.ateString.steps.title: Step 4: Monitor for Symptoms
catEmergency.ateString.steps.content: Watch for vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, and inability to defecate. These require emergency surgery.

catEmergency.ateString.faqs.question: Why is string dangerous for cats?
catEmergency.ateString.faqs.answer: String is a "linear foreign body" — it anchors at the base of the tongue or stomach and the rest is pulled through the intestines as they contract. This causes the intestines to "pleat" (bunch up) and the string can cut through the intestinal wall like a wire, causing perforation, peritonitis, and death.

catEmergency.ateString.faqs.question: What are the symptoms of string ingestion?
catEmergency.ateString.faqs.answer: Vomiting, loss of appetite, lethargy, drooling, visible string hanging from the mouth or anus, abdominal pain, and inability to defecate. If you see string, DO NOT pull it — this can cause more damage.

catEmergency.ateString.faqs.question: How is string ingestion treated?
catEmergency.ateString.faqs.answer: Treatment depends on location. If the string is still in the mouth/tongue, your vet may cut it. If it has entered the GI tract, surgery is often required to remove it safely. X-rays and ultrasound help determine the best approach.

compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.title: Cost-Effective
compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.body: Kibble costs $0.30–$0.80 per day for a 30kg dog, vs $1.50–$4.00 for wet food. Savings come from lower water content (10% vs 75%) and more efficient manufacturing.

compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.title: Dental Benefits
compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.body: The mechanical crunching action of hard kibble can help reduce tartar buildup. However, most dogs do not chew long enough for significant dental benefit — it is a bonus, not a substitute for brushing.

compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.title: Shelf-Stable & Convenient
compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.body: Unopened bags last 12–18 months at room temperature. No refrigeration needed, easy to store and travel with. Portioning is straightforward with a measuring cup.

compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.title: Energy-Dense
compare.dryVsWet.topicA.pros.body: With 350–450 kcal per 100g, kibble is ideal for large breeds or active dogs who need many calories without feeling full too quickly.

compare.dryVsWet.topicA.cons: Low moisture content (~10%) means dogs must drink separately; lower thirst drive can lead to chronic mild dehydration in some dogs.
Palatability can be lower than wet food; picky eaters may turn their nose up.
Quality varies enormously — some kibble relies heavily on grain fillers and plant proteins rather than animal-based proteins.

compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.title: High Moisture Content
compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.body: At 75–80% moisture, wet food provides significant hydration. This is especially beneficial for dogs with kidney issues, urinary crystals, or low thirst drive.

compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.title: Superior Palatability
compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.body: The aroma, texture, and fat content make wet food irresistible to most dogs. Ideal for picky eaters, senior dogs losing appetite, or convalescing pets.

compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.title: Lower Carbohydrates
compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.body: Quality wet foods often contain fewer grains and starches, with higher animal protein percentages. This more closely mimics a dog's ancestral diet.

compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.title: Easier to Eat for Senior Dogs
compare.dryVsWet.topicB.pros.body: Dogs with dental issues, missing teeth, or small mouths (e.g., Chihuahuas, Yorkies) find wet food much easier to consume than hard kibble.

compare.dryVsWet.topicB.cons: Cost: 3–5x more expensive per calorie than kibble for the same dog.
Shelf life: Once opened, canned food must be refrigerated and used within 3–5 days.
No dental crunch benefit — may contribute to faster tartar accumulation without other dental hygiene.
Bulky to store and heavier to transport.

compare.dryVsWet.faq.question: Can I mix dry and wet dog food?
compare.dryVsWet.faq.answer: Yes, mixing is safe and often recommended. A common approach is 75% kibble + 25% wet food by calorie. Calculate your dog's total daily calorie needs first, then split between the two. Ensure the combined diet meets AAFCO nutrient profiles — most complete & balanced kibble is formulated to be fed alone, so treat wet food as a supplement.

compare.dryVsWet.faq.question: Is wet food better for dogs with kidney disease?
compare.dryVsWet.faq.answer: Often yes. The high moisture content (75–80%) helps support kidney function by promoting hydration and flushing toxins. Dogs with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are frequently recommended higher-moisture diets by veterinary nutritionists. A prescription renal diet (wet or dry) may be needed in advanced cases.

compare.dryVsWet.faq.question: How much wet food replaces one cup of kibble?
compare.dryVsWet.faq.answer: Approximately 1 cup of kibble (100g, ~350 kcal) equals about 300–400g of wet food (~350 kcal). Always check the calorie content on the can label and adjust based on your dog's specific caloric needs. Use our Dog Calorie Calculator to determine the exact amount.

compare.dryVsWet.faq.question: Do dogs need wet food?
compare.dryVsWet.faq.answer: No, dogs do not need wet food if they are eating a complete and balanced dry diet and drinking adequate water. However, wet food provides meaningful benefits for hydration, palatability, and specific health conditions. It is a valuable tool in the dog owner's toolkit, not a necessity.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.title: Longer Lifespan
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.body: The average indoor-only cat lives 12–18 years, with many reaching 20+. This is 3–5x longer than the average outdoor cat, primarily due to reduced trauma and disease exposure.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.title: Lower Disease Risk
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.body: Indoor cats have minimal exposure to FeLV, FIV, FIP, and rabies from other cats. Parasite exposure is also significantly reduced.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.title: No Trauma Risk
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.body: No cars, no dog attacks, no fights with other cats, no predator encounters. The #1 cause of premature death in outdoor cats is vehicular trauma.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.title: Better Weight Control
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.pros.body: Indoor cats are fed measured meals rather than hunting or scavenging. Combined with our BCS tracker, obesity is more easily managed.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.cons: Environmental enrichment is mandatory — without it, indoor cats develop stress-related behaviors (urine marking, over-grooming, aggression).
Obesity is the #1 health risk for indoor cats, affecting 40–60% of indoor-only cats.
Needs significant owner time and resource investment (scratching posts, window perches, interactive play).

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.title: Natural Behavior Expression
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.body: Outdoor access allows climbing, hunting, territory patrolling, and sun-bathing — all core feline behaviors that are difficult to fully replicate indoors.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.title: Mental Stimulation
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.body: The outdoor environment provides endless sensory input. Outdoor cats rarely exhibit boredom-related behaviors seen in under-stimulated indoor cats.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.title: Exercise & Weight Management
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.body: Outdoor cats typically get more physical activity, making obesity less of a concern than with sedentary indoor cats.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.title: Reduced Litter Box Issues
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.pros.body: Cats with outdoor access rarely urinate or defecate outside the litter box, as they have the option to go outside.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.cons: Dramatically shorter lifespan: average 2–5 years for free-roaming outdoor cats.
High risk of vehicular trauma, predation (coyotes, dogs), poisoning (rodenticides), and fighting injuries.
Exposure to infectious diseases: FeLV, FIV, FIP, rabies, and parasites.
Neighborhood conflict — digging in gardens, hunting wildlife (ecological impact), and conflicts with other cats or pets.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.faq.question: Is it cruel to keep a cat indoors?
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.faq.answer: No — with proper environmental enrichment, indoor cats live longer, healthier lives. Cats do not have the same drive for outdoor access as dogs. Key needs: vertical space (cat trees), scratching posts, puzzle feeders, window perches with a view, and 15–20 minutes of daily interactive play. This satisfies their core behavioral needs entirely.

compare.indoorVsOutdoor.faq.question: How do I transition an outdoor cat to indoor?
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.faq.answer: Gradual transition over 2–4 weeks is most effective.
